title.en: Ramayana — Yuddha Kanda (Wikipedia Simplified Story — English, Full Text)

lessons.title: Lesson 01 — Preparation for War
lessons.content:
For the immense favor done by Hanuman, Rama embraced him and said, "No one else could have accomplished such a difficult task. You are the confidant who saved all our lives. There is no other messenger like you. What reward can I give you other than a tight embrace?" Sugriva consoled and reassured the sorrowful Rama, affirming that Rama's victory was certain. Hanuman then comprehensively explained the defense system of the city of Lanka. Following a discussion, everyone resolved to proceed with the war.

At an opportune moment, the colossal Vanara army, under the leadership of Neela, loudly set out towards the south. On Rama's command, the army marched through forests, hills, mountains, rivers, and lakes, avoiding populated areas. Neela was the army chief for this host moving under Rama's command, and Sugriva was its ruler. Rama rode on Hanuman's shoulders, and Lakshmana rode on Angada's shoulders. Many great heroes like Jambavan, Sushena, Vegadarshi, Shatabali, Kesari, Panasa, Gaja, Arka, Valimukha, Prajangha, Jambha, and Rabhasa advanced, exciting the Vanara and Bhalluka army. The army, eager to accomplish Rama's mission with valor, resembled another ocean as it reached the seashore. The Vanara (monkey) warriors camped in one place, the Golangoola (gorilla) warriors in another, and the Bhalluka (bear) warriors in a third, dividing into three sections.

lessons.title: Lesson 02 — Vibhishana Seeks Refuge
lessons.content:
In Lanka, Ravana began consulting with his advisors about the war. He ordered that the city's security be tightened. The Rakshasa (demon) warriors praised Ravana's might and their own capabilities, assuring him that they had nothing to fear. Each boasted that they could personally eliminate Rama and Lakshmana. However, Ravana's younger brother, **Vibhishana**, disagreed. He tried to convince Ravana that the fire of Rama and Lakshmana's wrath would surely consume Lanka and that Ravana had carelessly tied the serpent of Sita around his own neck. He advised him to correct his mistake by returning Sita to Rama. He went to Ravana's palace again, reporting numerous bad omens plaguing Lanka and imploring him to save the Rakshasa race from the impending disaster.

The next day, when Ravana held court in the council chamber, **Kumbhakarna** was also present along with all the ministers and relatives. Kumbhakarna conceded that Ravana had made a mistake but promised to fight valiantly to secure his brother's objective. When Vibhishana tried to offer good counsel again, Indrajit and Ravana harshly rebuked him. Taking leave of his elder brother, Vibhishana, along with his four devoted Rakshasa associates, flew into the sky, crossed the ocean, and sought **refuge with Rama**. The Vanara chiefs advised Rama not to trust him. Hanuman, however, stated that Vibhishana was gentle and trustworthy. Rama, declaring that protecting all beings who seek refuge with him was his solemn vow, granted asylum to Vibhishana. Vibhishana then detailed the prowess of mighty warriors like Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Indrajit, and Prahasta, as well as the strength of the city of Lanka. Rama swore an oath upon his three brothers that he would not return to Ayodhya until he had killed Ravana, along with his sons and relatives. Rama then performed the **abhisheka** (consecration) of Vibhishana as the future King of Lanka with the waters of the ocean.

lessons.title: Lesson 03 — The Bridge Across the Ocean
lessons.content:
Ravana sent a messenger named Shuka to Sugriva, attempting diplomacy by claiming that they had no quarrel and asking him not to help Rama. Sugriva replied, "Ravana! Since you have done me no favor, you are not dear to me. Since you are Rama's enemy, you are my enemy too. There is no power in the three worlds that can protect one who has incurred Rama's wrath." Hanuman and Sugriva then asked Vibhishana for a way to cross the ocean. Vibhishana advised Rama to humbly request the aid of the **Ocean God** (Samudra Deva). Rama vowed to fast and prayed to the Ocean God for three nights, but the deity did not appear. Angered, Rama prepared to fire an arrow to dry up the entire ocean. The Ocean God appeared, respectfully bowed, and explained that he could not abandon his nature (water) but suggested that the bridge could be built with the skill of **Nala**, the son of Vishwakarma. At the Ocean God's request, Rama discharged his Astra at the dacoits in Drumakulya.

The extraordinary work of building a bridge across the ocean began under the supervision of Nala. The Vanaras built a bridge 14 *yojanas* (leagues) long on the first day, 20 on the second, 21 on the third, 22 on the fourth, and 23 on the fifth. Thus, in **five days**, a bridge **100 *yojanas*** long and **10 *yojanas*** wide was completed. Vibhishana stood guard over the bridge. The Vanara and Bhalluka armies, along with Rama and Lakshmana, crossed the bridge and reached Lanka. The army, led by Neela, resembled another ocean, ready for Rama's mission. They set up camp in an area rich with fruits, roots, and water.

From a distance, the city of Lanka, situated on the Trikuta mountain, appeared majestic, as if created by Vishwakarma's mere thought. Rama was astonished by its splendor. However, omens indicated to Rama that the impending war was destined to soak the earth in blood. He directed his army to be vigilant and laid out his strategy. He then released Shuka, a messenger who had been held captive.

lessons.title: Lesson 04 — The Valiant Bear and Vanara Army
lessons.content:
Ravana's spies, Shuka and Sarana, explained the prowess of heroes like Rama, Lakshmana, Sugriva, Jambavan, and Hanuman to Ravana. They stated that it was impossible to count the number of Vanara forces and suggested that returning Sita to Rama would be wise. They were then taken to the top of the palace to view the main commanders of the Vanara army:

**Neela**, the supreme commander of all Vanara forces, was roaring like a lion alongside thousands of army chiefs. **Angada** was as mighty as his father and was determined to ensure Rama's victory. **Nala** was the great one who built the bridge over the ocean. **Shweta**, renowned in the three worlds, shone like silver. **Kumuda**, who loved war, came from the Gomati riverbank. **Rambha**, who was copper-colored, came from the Vindhya mountains. **Sharaba**, with his ears pricked up, was fearless of death. **Panasa**, who resembled a mountain, came from Pariyatra, and **Vinata** came from the banks of the Krishna River with armies in the millions. The immensely powerful **Krodha** came with 60 *lakhs* of troops, and the huge, ochre-colored **Gavaya** came with 70 *lakhs* of troops. The commander **Haras**, who arrived with crores of followers, was a fearsome fighter.

**Dhoomra**, the leader who came from the Rikshavanta region on the Narmada riverbank with countless Bhallukas that looked like antimony mountains, was terrifying. Dhoomra's younger brother, **Jambavan**, assisted Indra in the war between the Devas and Asuras. **Dambha**, a famous Vanara warrior, was very strong. The great-grandfather of the Vanaras, **Sannada**, who looked like a mountain, once caused Indra himself to retreat when they clashed. **Kradhana**, who came from the Himalayas with ten crore warriors, was undefeated. **Pramadhi**, who enjoyed attacking elephants, and his followers were eager to attack Lanka. **Gavaksha** and crores of other Vanaras were still crossing the bridge. **Kesari** was the lord of the Vanaras who came from Mount Meru. **Shatabali**, the leader of the fierce Vanaras who looked like venomous serpents, came from the Kanchan Mountain region. The numerical strength of the Vanaras under **Gaja**, **Gavaksha**, **Gavaya**, **Nala**, and **Neela** was countless. The Vanara heroes who did not transgress Sugriva's command were immensely powerful, invincible, and could change their form at will.

The brothers **Mainda** and **Dwivida** attained immortality through the grace of Brahma. The brothers **Sumukha** and **Durdhara** were the sons of the God of Death. **Hanuman**, the son of Kesari and Vayu Deva, was unmatched in the three worlds. When angered, he could churn the ocean. **Rama**, who was learned in the Vedas and Vedangas, upheld Dharma, was dark-skinned like a cloud, and had lotus eyes, but his wrath was equal to death itself. **Lakshmana** was intelligent, had uncontrollable anger, was ready to sacrifice his life for his brother, and his arrows never missed their mark. Your brother, **Vibhishana**, stands by Rama's side, and Rama has already coronated him as the King of Lanka. **Sugriva**, the lord of all monkeys, rules Kishkindha. He is greater than all the Vanaras, like the Himalayas, and is dedicated to uniting Sita and Rama. Thus, the Vanaras, in groups of millions and *mahaughas* (an ancient measure of number), have come to attack Lanka.

Another spy sent by Ravana, **Shardoola**, confirmed the same. He gave further details about the prowess of the Vanara and Bhalluka heroes: **Sugriva** was the son of Riksharajas; **Dhoomra** and **Jambavan** were the sons of Gadgadu; **Kesari** was the son of Brihaspati; **Sushena** was the son of Varuna; **Dadhivaktra** was the son of Chandra; **Sumukha**, **Durmukha**, and **Vegadarshi** were aspects of Krittanta (Death); **Neela** was the son of Pavaka (Fire); **Hanuman** was the son of Vayu; **Angada** was the grandson of Puruhuta (Indra); **Mainda** and **Dwivida** were born from the parts of the Ashwini Devas; **Gaja**, **Gavaksha**, **Gavaya**, **Gandhamadana**, and **Sharaba** were like the sons of Samavarti (Yama); **Shweta** and **Jyotirmukha** were the sons of Bhaskara (Sun); **Hemakoota** was the son of Varuna; **Nala** was the son of the Divine Architect (Vishwakarma); and **Durdhara** was the son of Vasu. All of them were born from divine parts and were eager for war. Rama killed fourteen thousand Rakshasas, including Khara and Dushana, all at once. Lakshmana was an equal match to him. Vibhishana was the only wise one among the Rakshasas. Thus, facing this mobilized army, it was up to Ravana to choose between victory or heroic death.

lessons.title: Lesson 05 — Before the War
lessons.content:
Ravana summoned a sorcerer named **Vidyujjihva** and had him create a **magical head** resembling Rama's, along with a bow and arrows. He showed this illusion to Sita, telling her that Rama, Lakshmana, and the Vanara army had been destroyed in the war. Sita burst into tears. After Ravana left, Vibhishana's wife, a virtuous woman named **Sarama**, consoled Sita, explaining that it was an illusion and that she had overheard the truth in secret. She assured Sita that Rama was ready for battle with the Bhalluka and Vanara forces, and her time of happiness was near, as Ravana's destruction was inevitable.

**Malyavan**, an aged Rakshasa who was the brother of Ravana's maternal grandfather, tried to advise Ravana to stop the war. Ravana harshly insulted him. Ravana knew that the Vanara army and Rama-Lakshmana were invincible and unparalleled. Yet, he believed that the Rakshasa army, led by **Prahasta**, was also undefeated. His confidence was that Prahasta, Indrajit, and Nikumbha alone could surely eliminate Rama and Lakshmana, making it unnecessary for even the mighty **Kumbhakarna** (who treated Indra's Vajra as a blade of grass) or himself to enter the battle.

Ravana mobilized his army and made strong arrangements for defense everywhere. **Prahasta** was stationed at the East Gate, **Mahaparshwa** and **Mahodara** at the South, **Indrajit** at the West, and **Shuka** and **Sarana** at the North. **Virupaksha** was in the center of Lanka. Ravana himself declared he would supervise the North Gate, among other places. Rama learned all this through Vibhishana's spies. Rama then directed **Neela** to lead his army toward the East Gate, **Angada** toward the South, and **Hanuman** toward the West. He announced that he himself would march toward the North Gate. **Sugriva**, **Jambavan**, and **Vibhishana** were to remain in the center to manage everything. After making these arrangements, Rama ascended the Suvela peak with his main commanders to survey the city of Lanka. Ravana appeared on the top of a tower in the distance. Seeing him, Sugriva, filled with rage, leaped across and engaged in a fierce wrestling match. As Ravana prepared to use his magical powers, Sugriva leaped back with a single jump.

At Rama's command, **Angada** went as a messenger to give Ravana one last message from Rama: If Ravana surrendered Sita and sought refuge, Rama would forgive him. Ravana scornfully rejected Angada. Angada then kicked and destroyed the pinnacle of Ravana's tower and returned.

lessons.title: Lesson 06 — Victory for Rama, Lakshmana, and Sugriva
lessons.content:
The Vanara army then besieged Lanka. First, they filled the moat with dirt, boulders, and trees, and then occupied the ramparts. They destroyed the towers, ramparts, and arched gateways. Virabahu, Subahu, and Nala began to breach the ramparts. Kumuda, Praghana, and Panasa attacked the East Gate; Shatabali attacked the South; Sushena attacked the West; and Mahakaya, Gavaksha, and Dhoomra attacked the North. The Rakshasa army, like the sea at the time of cosmic dissolution, or like black clouds, roared like lions and countered the Vanaras with the sound of *dundubhi* drums. The intense battle caused the earth and the interspace to tremble. In an instant, the battle turned fierce, and the ground was covered with blood and flesh.

**Duel battles** began between the prominent Vanara and Rakshasa heroes. Angada fought Indrajit; Sampati (Vibhishana's minister) fought Prajangha; Hanuman fought Jambumali; Vibhishana fought Shatrughna; Gaja fought Tapana; Neela fought Nikumbha; Sugriva fought Praghassa; Lakshmana fought Virupaksha; Mainda fought Vajramushti; Dwivida fought Ashaniprabha; Nala fought Pratapana; and Sushena fought Vidyunmali. Rakshasas named Agniketu, Rashmiketu, Suptaghna, and Madhyakopa surrounded Rama but were killed by him. The war continued even at night, with blood flowing like rivers. It became a cosmic night of destruction.

lessons.title: Lesson 07 — Release from the Naga-Pasha
lessons.content:
Defeated by Angada, **Indrajit** suddenly vanished. He initiated a magical war and used the **Naga-Astra** (serpent weapon) to render Rama and Lakshmana helpless, striking terror into the enemy army. Every inch of Rama and Lakshmana's bodies was covered with arrows. The Vanara army fled in shame. All the Vanara commanders were wounded by Indrajit's arrows. Indrajit, triumphant, went to his father, boasting that he had killed Rama and Lakshmana and disabled the Vanara army, as the bonds of the Naga-Astra were inescapable. Ravana rejoiced and ordered that the 'corpses' of the Raghavas be shown to Sita. Sita was brought on the Pushpaka Vimana to see the sight and began to weep. **Trijata** consoled Sita, assuring her that Rama and Lakshmana were only momentarily disabled and would soon recover.

Frightened Vanaras gathered around the Raghavas, mourning and worrying that the Rakshasas might return. Rama, regaining a little consciousness, was deeply troubled upon seeing Lakshmana, lamented that all his vows were now false, and prepared to fast until death (*Prayopavesha*). He thanked the Vanaras for their help and asked them to return, saying that they had done their duty as friends with all their might, but the will of God could not be violated. All the Vanaras wept. Vibhishana was heartbroken upon seeing Rama and Lakshmana lying on a bed of arrows. Sugriva, however, consoled Vibhishana, assuring him of his future kingship of Lanka. He instructed his father-in-law, **Sushena**, to take Rama and Lakshmana back to Kishkindha. Sugriva then vowed to destroy Ravana along with his sons and relatives and rescue Sita himself. Sushena suggested that if Sampati, Panasa, and Hanuman could bring the divine herbs (*Divya Aushadhas*), it would be beneficial.

Just as everyone was dejected, a great storm blew, churning the ocean. **Garuda**, the great eagle, arrived like a strong wind. With his arrival, the serpents that were holding Rama and Lakshmana captive in the form of arrows all fled. Garuda touched all of Rama and Lakshmana's limbs with his hands. Immediately, their wounds vanished, and they gained even more radiance, strength, valor, and prowess than before. Garuda embraced them and said, "Be vigilant. You will learn later how I became your friend. Rama! It is certain that you will destroy Lanka, kill Ravana, and recover Sita." After circumambulating Rama and Lakshmana, he flew into the sky.

lessons.title: Lesson 08 — Deaths of Rakshasa Warriors
lessons.content:
With Rama and Lakshmana recovered, the Vanaras began leaping with joy, roaring like lions, prancing, and uprooting trees, preparing for battle. The astonished Ravana sent **Dhoomraksha** to the war. Dhoomraksha, along with a large army, went to the South Gate and began slaughtering the Vanaras. Every Vanara hero proclaimed his name and began beating the Rakshasas. Dhoomraksha was crushed under a large mountain peak thrown by **Hanuman**.

Sighing at Dhoomraksha's death, Ravana ordered the great, brave, and magical warrior **Vajradamshtra** to go to war. Vajradamshtra's army marched toward the South Gate, appearing like moving mountains. The fierce battle that ensued filled the battlefield with corpses, limbs, weapons, armor, and ornaments. Vultures, eagles, and jackals began feasting on the blood-soaked body parts. The Rakshasas trembled before **Angada's** onslaught. Angada and Vajradamshtra engaged in a fierce fistfight. Finally, Angada severed Vajradamshtra's head. The Rakshasas fled back into Lanka.

Next, the mighty warrior **Akampana** set out for battle with enthusiasm, leading an army like the sea. Vanaras and Rakshasas fought fiercely, with neither side giving ground. The cloud of dust that initially rose eventually settled due to the rivers of blood. Akampana began destroying the Vanaras who enthusiastically surrounded the Rakshasas with a rain of arrows. **Hanuman** stopped him. The earth trembled at Hanuman's foot strike. Hanuman uprooted a massive tree and crushed Akampana with it. The Rakshasas all fled into the city, pushing and trampling each other.

Ravana then asked Prahasta what should be done. **Prahasta** was Ravana's army chief, an expert in weapons, and a great hero. He had previously advised Ravana that returning Sita was the safest course of action. Now, stating that his life's purpose was to repay Ravana's affection, Prahasta completed his sacrificial rites (*Homadi*), harnessed his great chariot with the serpent banner, assembled a massive army terrifying to the enemy, and set out for the East Gate. He was accompanied by capable followers: Narantaka, Kumbhahanu, Mahanada, and Samunnata. The Rakshasa and Vanara heroes clashed, slapping their arms. The roars and wails of both sides shook the heavens and the earth.

**Dwivida** killed Narantaka by striking him with a mountain peak. **Durmukha** beat Samunnata down with a large tree. **Jambavan** crushed Mahavada with a massive stone. **Tara** beat Kumbhahanu to the ground with a large tree. Prahasta simultaneously slaughtered many Vanara heroes. The battlefield became a landscape of red mountains made of Vanara and Rakshasa corpses, with rivers of blood flowing between them. **Neela** leaped at Prahasta like a whirlwind onto a cloud. They grappled like rutting elephants. With a large boulder, Neela smashed Prahasta's head, killing him. The Rakshasa army fled into Lanka like a broken river dam.

lessons.title: Lesson 09 — Ravana's Defeat
lessons.content:
Realizing the futility of relying on others, **Ravana** himself set out for battle on a divine chariot, accompanied by a host of mighty Rakshasa warriors. His army was like moving antimony mountains. At the forefront were Akampana, blazing like the sun; Indrajit, wielding a great bow; Mahodara, built like the Vindhya mountain; Pishacha, like a thunderbolt; Trishiras, holding a lightning-like spear; Kumbha, with a serpent banner; Nikumbha, holding a mace studded with diamonds; and Narantaka, riding a chariot of fire—all eager for battle. In their midst, Ravana, holding a white umbrella, shone like a blazing sun. Rama was astonished by Ravana's splendor. Declaring that Ravana's end was near due to the sin of abducting Sita, Rama strung his bow.

Ravana sent the remaining Rakshasa leaders back to guard Lanka. He began scattering the Vanara army with his arrows, which were like venomous serpents. Sugriva was rendered unconscious. Ravana pulverized the mountain peaks thrown by Gavaksha, Rishabha, Gavaya, Jyotirmukha, and Nala. Ravana was shaken by Hanuman's slap, and Hanuman was shaken by Ravana's punch. **Neela**, assuming a minute form, annoyed Ravana. Since Neela was the son of Agni (Fire), Ravana's Agneya-Astra (Fire Weapon) could not harm him. Lakshmana's arrows broke Ravana's bow. Ravana's **Shakti** weapon struck Lakshmana, who lost consciousness. Ravana tried but failed to lift Lakshmana. **Hanuman** lifted Lakshmana and laid him near Rama. A punch from Hanuman caused Ravana to vomit blood and faint. Recovering his senses, Ravana resumed his arrow attack.

Rama ascended Hanuman's shoulders and continued fighting Ravana. Hanuman was unfazed by Ravana's sharp arrows. In the fierce battle that followed, Ravana's chariot, horses, umbrella, and banner were destroyed. His crown fell to the ground, and his bow slipped from his hand. Rama told Ravana to take a rest and return for battle the next day. **Ravana** retreated into Lanka, filled with shame.

lessons.title: Lesson 10 — The Death of Kumbhakarna
lessons.content:
Overwhelmed with shame, Ravana sent his ministers to awaken his brother, **Kumbhakarna**. They used *bheri* drums, pricked him with spears, hit him with maces, and had elephants trample him before finally waking him from his sleep. Upon waking, Kumbhakarna heartily ate masses of meat, drank pots of blood, and belched. Learning the situation, he bathed, adorned himself, drank pots of strong liquor, and went to Ravana. Just by his walking through the city, the Vanara armies scattered in fear. Vibhishana explained that there was no other hero in the Rakshasa race as great as him. The Vanaras were eventually calmed by being told that Kumbhakarna was a mere machine, not a real Rakshasa.

Ravana explained the situation to Kumbhakarna. Kumbhakarna, with brotherly affection, criticized Ravana's thoughtless wicked deeds. He was also displeased with Mahodara's suggestion to trick Sita with deceit. He vowed to rectify the situation by devouring Rama, Lakshmana, and the entire Vanara army. He promised Ravana and, blazing like fire, grabbed his mace (*Parigha*), which resembled the noose of Yama, crossed the city wall in a single stride, and went out to war. The Vanara armies started fleeing upon seeing the massive warrior, who was six hundred bow-lengths tall and one hundred feet in circumference. **Angada** somehow managed to stop them by giving them courage.

Kumbhakarna began to slaughter the Vanara army, crushing and swallowing them like a fire consuming a dry forest. Mountain peaks thrown by Angada, Rishabha, Sharabha, Mainda, and Neela shattered against Kumbhakarna's body. He began chewing and swallowing hundreds of Vanaras. A blow from **Hanuman** caused Kumbhakarna to vomit blood. A strike from Kumbhakarna's spear caused Hanuman to vomit blood. The heroes like Angada who faced the Rakshasa fell unconscious just from his forceful shaking. **Sugriva** put his knee across Kumbhakarna's spear and broke it. Sugriva then lost consciousness after being hit by a mountain peak thrown by Kumbhakarna. Kumbhakarna seized the unconscious Sugriva and carried him toward Lanka. Sugriva regained consciousness, shook himself free, bit off the Rakshasa's nose and ears, and leaped back into the Vanara army.

Kumbhakarna returned, maddened, and began killing everyone indiscriminately. Rama's arrow, which had killed Vali, proved ineffective against Kumbhakarna. Finally, the arrows of Rama and Lakshmana left Kumbhakarna weaponless. Rama cut off his hands with the Vayuvyastra (Wind Weapon) and the Aindrastra (Indra's Weapon). He cut off his thighs with two other powerful arrows. But even then, the hero came forward with his mouth open, like Rahu, until Rama killed him with the **Aindrastra**. He fell like a mountain, and many Vanaras and Rakshasas perished beneath him.

lessons.title: Lesson 11 — More Deaths of Rakshasa Warriors
lessons.content:
To console the grieving Ravana, his sons **Devantaka**, **Narantaka**, **Atikaya**, and **Trishiras**, along with Ravana's brothers **Matta** and **Unmatta**—all great heroes—set out for battle the next day. They were accompanied by Mahodara and Mahaparshwa. The war between the Vanara and Rakshasa heroes became fierce again. The battlefield was soon covered with Vanara corpses due to Narantaka's fierce onslaught. At Sugriva's command, **Angada** leaped at Narantaka. A punch from Angada caused Narantaka to vomit blood, thrash about, and die.

At Narantaka's death, Devantaka, Trishiras, and Mahodara rushed toward Angada in grief. Angada fought all three without faltering. Hanuman and Neela came to Angada's aid. Devantaka's head was smashed by **Hanuman's** punch, and he died. **Neela** killed Mahodara by striking him with a great mountain. Hanuman shattered the powerful spear thrown by Trishiras. With a single stroke of Trishiras's own sharp sword, Hanuman cut off his three heads. **Rishabha** seized Mahaparshwa's mace and smashed his head with it. The fear-stricken Rakshasa army all fled back into Lanka.

lessons.title: Lesson 12 — Hanuman Brings the Oshadhi Mountain
lessons.content:
Consoling Ravana, who was deeply saddened by the death of his sons and brothers, **Indrajit** went to the battlefield. He performed a *homa* (sacrificial rite), consecrated his weapons, and became **invisible**. He began slaughtering the Vanara army with sharp arrows. All the Vanara heroes lost consciousness. Then, Indrajit launched the **Brahma-Astra**. Everyone fainted. Rama, Lakshmana, and Hanuman also had to respect the Brahma-Astra. Believing everyone was dead, Indrajit roared triumphantly and returned to Lanka.

Vibhishana and Hanuman began searching among the seemingly dead for anyone alive. **Jambavan**, recovering slightly, asked, "Is Anjana's son, Hanuman, still alive?" Surprised, Vibhishana listened as Jambavan explained, "If Hanuman is alive, the Vanara army, even if dead, will surely live again. If the opposite is true, we are as good as dead even if we are alive! We only have hope for life if Hanuman, who is equal to Vayu (Wind) in speed and Agni (Fire) in prowess, is with us." Jambavan then asked Hanuman to bring the potent herbs **Mrita Sanjeevani**, **Vishalyakarani**, **Sauvarnakarani**, and **Sandhanakarani** from the **Oshadhiparvata** (Herb Mountain) in the Himalayas.

At Jambavan's request, Hanuman bowed to Rama and the ocean, grew to the size of a mountain, and shot up into the sky like a *Sudarsana* (disc). He went to the Sanjeevani mountain via the sky and began searching for the herbs. Since he could not identify the herbs, Hanuman uprooted the entire mountain and, shining like another sun in the sky, brought it to the battlefield. Rama, Lakshmana, and the Vanaras all regained consciousness. Even the Vanaras who had died were revived. However, since Ravana had commanded that the dead Rakshasas be thrown into the sea immediately, the Rakshasas gained no benefit. Hanuman then took the mountain back and replaced it in its original location.

Following Sugriva's command, the Vanaras entered the city of Lanka with firebrands and set the city ablaze.

lessons.title: Lesson 13 — The Deaths of Kumbha and Nikumbha
lessons.content:
The enraged Ravana sent **Kumbha** and **Nikumbha**, the sons of Kumbhakarna, to battle. They were accompanied by **Yupaksha**, **Shonitaksha**, **Prajangha**, and **Kampana**—all great warriors. The Vanara army surrounded them. Kampana was crushed under a mountain peak thrown by **Angada** and died.

Shonitaksha, Yupaksha, and Prajangha leaped toward Angada. **Mainda** and **Dwivida** stood by Angada's side. A terrible battle ensued among the six. Angada snatched Prajangha's sword and severed his head with it. Dwivida scratched Shonitaksha's face completely and pinned him to the ground. Mainda seized Yupaksha, pinned him down, and squeezed his neck.

Kumbha, with renewed fury, shot arrows that rendered Mainda and Dwivida unconscious. Seeing his uncles fall, Angada leaped at Kumbha. A punch from Kumbha caused Angada to also faint. Thereupon, **Sugriva** entered the battle, and a fierce hand-to-hand combat took place for a long time. Finally, Sugriva's fist-blows killed **Kumbha**.

**Nikumbha** charged toward the Vanaras with a great mace (*Parigha*). It struck **Hanuman's** chest and shattered into pieces. Hanuman's punch cracked Nikumbha's armor. They exchanged blows. Finally, Hanuman grabbed Nikumbha's head, twisted his neck, and broke it. The Vanaras leaped with joy, and the Rakshasas were terrified.

Ravana fainted upon hearing the news of Kumbha and Nikumbha's deaths. Recovering, he sent **Makarāksha**, the son of Khara, to battle. He led an army of many shape-shifting Rakshasas. Makarāksha intended to take revenge on Rama, who had killed his father in the Dandaka Forest. A fierce battle between the Vanaras and Rakshasas resumed. Makarāksha was consumed by **Rama's** Pavaka-Astra (Fire Weapon) and turned to ash.

lessons.title: Lesson 14 — The Death of Indrajit
lessons.content:
Hearing that Kumbha, Nikumbha, and Makarāksha had fallen, Ravana was overcome with sorrow, rage, and fear. He blessed **Indrajit** and sent him to the battlefield, asking him to avenge his pain by killing the humans and Vanaras. Indrajit performed a *homa*, donned his weapons, and came to the battlefield in an **invisible form**, devastating the Vanara army and harassing Rama and Lakshmana with sharp arrows. Rama advised Lakshmana against using the Brahma-Astra. In the meantime, Indrajit, becoming visible, severed the head of an illusory Sita (*Maya Sita*) in front of everyone. Everyone plunged into grief. Vibhishana, knowing Ravana's nature, convinced them it was merely an illusion. Indrajit had gone to **Nikumbhila** to perform a sacrifice (*Yaga*). Rakshasas were arrayed around him like a protective formation.

Vibhishana explained that Indrajit's death was destined to be at the hands of whomever could prevent him from completing the *Yaga* at Nikumbhila. With Rama's permission, **Lakshmana**, armed, ascended Hanuman's shoulders and, along with Jambavan, Vibhishana, and Angada, moved toward Nikumbhila. After a fearsome battle, they broke through the surrounding Rakshasas and confronted Indrajit. Indrajit stopped the *homa*, cursed Vibhishana as a traitor, and, taking the form of the Destroyer (Kalāntaka), began to fight Lakshmana. Lakshmana, a disciple of Vishwamitra, answered him appropriately. In the fierce battle, arrows covered the sky. Soumitri (Lakshmana) launched the **Maheshwara-Astra** (Shiva's Weapon) with the chant: "If Rama, of the Ikshvaku lineage, is the embodiment of Dharma and a keeper of his word, may this Maheshwara-Astra slay Indrajit!" The Astra severed Indrajit's head. The Rakshasas fled. The Vanaras cheered for Lakshmana, danced, and reached Rama.

lessons.title: Lesson 15 — The Commencement of the Rama-Ravana War
lessons.content:
Ravana fainted upon Indrajit's death. Rising, he intended to kill Sita out of rage. A wise minister named **Supārshwa** stopped him, advising him to fight heroically and achieve victory. Ravana, desperate, entered the battlefield through the North Gate with Mahodara, Mahaparshwa, Virupaksha, and other great heroes and the army. The Vanara heroes charged forward to face the Rakshasas, cheering with excitement and shouting the names of victory: "Victory to Sri Ramachandra!" "Victory to Lakshmana!" "Victory to Sugriva!" "Victory to Hanuman!" "Victory to Angada!" "Victory to Jambavan!"

Ravana's terribly fierce arrows scattered the Vanara army. Virupaksha also joined the onslaught. Ravana charged at Rama, and Virupaksha began destroying the Vanaras. **Sugriva** raged like a storm at the time of cosmic dissolution, throwing mountain after mountain and scattering many Rakshasa heroes. When Virupaksha tried to stop him, Sugriva delivered a single slap to his face, causing Virupaksha to vomit blood and die. Then, **Mahodara**, with incredible valor, began cutting down the Vanaras. Sugriva stopped him, and a brutal wrestling match ensued between them. Sugriva's blow smashed Mahodara's head. **Mahaparshwa** began savagely tearing apart the Vanaras with his sword. Angada confronted him with an iron mace. Jambavan and Gavaksha broke Mahaparshwa's chariot and killed his horses. A blow from Angada killed Mahaparshwa.

lessons.title: Lesson 16 — Lakshmana Faints, Maruthi's Service
lessons.content:
Ravana began to torment Rama and Lakshmana with his sharp arrows. Lakshmana severed the head of Ravana's charioteer, broke his bow, and shattered Ravana's banner, which was painted with a human head. Vibhishana killed Ravana's horses. Lakshmana neutralized the Astra and Shakti weapons that Ravana hurled at Vibhishana. The Vanaras cheered.

The **Shakti** weapon hurled by Ravana struck Lakshmana's chest, and he **fainted**. Rama, grieving over his brother's condition, raged like the fire of cosmic dissolution and began raining arrows on Ravana. After a while, the Shakti weapon left Lakshmana. Rama then addressed his followers: "You protect Soumitri and watch the battle. I will show you who Rama is. The world must become *Aravanam* (without Ravana)." The Rama-Ravana war intensified. After fighting for a long time, Ravana flew into the air, entered a cloud, and retreated into Lanka.

Rama wept upon seeing Lakshmana lying lifeless on the battlefield. Sushena consoled him, assuring him that Lakshmana had only fainted, and instructed Hanuman to return to the mountain peak. Hanuman flew with the speed of Garuda. Unable to identify the herbs, he uprooted the entire mountain and brought it back with the Oshadhis (herbs). Sushena selected the herbs, extracted the juice, and poured it onto Lakshmana's tongue. Lakshmana regained consciousness, and Rama hugged him, weeping. Lakshmana stood up and said, "Brother! First, fulfill your vow. Can an enemy survive after falling under your gaze? Ravana must be destroyed before the sun sets this evening!"

lessons.title: Lesson 17 — The Slaying of Ravana
lessons.content:
At that moment, **Matali**, sent by Indra, arrived as a charioteer with a divine chariot. The chariot contained a fire-like armor, Indra's bow (*Aindra-Chapa*), sun-like arrows, and a sharp *Shakti* weapon. Rama rejoiced, circumambulated the chariot, and ascended it. Ravana returned to battle with a diamond-like spear. The spear thrown by Ravana incinerated the arrows sent by Rama. Rama then hurled the **Indra-Shakti** brought by Matali, which destroyed Ravana's spear. Ravana also flooded Rama with a barrage of arrows. Rama's fierce arrows left Ravana's body soaked in blood. Finally, observing Ravana weaponless, his charioteer drove the chariot away.

**Agastya** arrived and instructed the battle-weary Rama in the **Aditya Hridaya**, an ancient, highly secret mantra. This mantra, which praises the Sun, the witness to all worlds, grants victory, is inexhaustible, supremely auspicious, destroys all sins, calms worry and sorrow, increases longevity, and removes all dangers. Rama purified himself (*Achamisi*), chanted the king of mantras three times, and bowed to Aditya (the Sun), the lord of the luminous bodies, the day-maker, the auspicious victor, the thousand-rayed, the destroyer of darkness, and the vanquisher of foes. He prepared for battle, holding his bow, determined to slay Ravana.

Ravana's charioteer brought his chariot back before Rama. The chariot, which was fully equipped with weapons and resembled a Gandharva city, approached in a counter-clockwise direction (*Apradakshinanga*). Realizing that Ravana's death was imminent, Rama instructed Matali to drive their chariot in a clockwise direction (*Pradakshina Marga*). Rama and Ravana exerted all their power, raining arrows upon each other. Their arrows covered the sky. The Devas proclaimed, "The Rama-Ravana war is like the Rama-Ravana war" (meaning it has no equal). Their chariots darted across the battlefield. Rama's arrows brought down Ravana's banner, and his horses were killed.

Ravana's head was severed by Rama's arrows, which were like great serpents, but another immediately grew back. Even after Rama cut off Ravana's heads one hundred and one times, they continued to regenerate. "Rama! This is not the way. Launch the **Brahma-Astra**," urged Matali. Rama then drew the Brahma-Astra given to him by Agastya. It shone like a hissing serpent. The wind was in its wings, Agni and Surya were in its tip, and Mount Meru and Mount Mandara were its presiding deities in its weight. Its body was Brahma-like. Rama consecrated the divine weapon with Vedic chants, drew the bow taut with a focused mind, and released it. The Brahma-Astra, like a thunderbolt released from Rama's thunderbolt-like hands with adamantine resolve, spewed fire, pierced Ravana's heart, became smeared with his blood, entered the earth for pacification, and quietly returned to Rama's quiver. Rama, with reddened eyes, a body covered in the wounds of arrows, and the radiance of a crore suns, rested his bow on the ground and, holding an arrow in his other hand, shone as the embodiment of heroic fortune, praised by the lords of the three worlds. All the Devas offered salutations to Rama. Sugriva, Vibhishana, Angada, Lakshmana, and other friends worshipped the victorious Rama in the prescribed manner.

lessons.title: Lesson 18 — Sita's Agni Pariksha (Fire Ordeal)
lessons.content:
Ravana was killed in the fierce battle. At Rama's command, Vibhishana performed Ravana's final rites. Vibhishana was then crowned King. With Vibhishana's permission, Hanuman entered Lanka and reported the news of victory to Sita. Vibhishana's inner palace retinue had Sita take an auspicious bath and brought her to Rama in a palanquin.

Rama spoke harshly: "Sita, I fought this war for the honor of the Ikshvaku lineage. Since Ravana looked at you with an evil eye, I cannot accept you. You appear to me as painful as a lamp to eyes afflicted with a malady. You are free to go wherever you please." Sita burst into tears of grief. "O son of a noble man, O greatest of heroes, you speak like an ordinary man. The sin of Ravana touching me is not mine; it is the will of fate. My heart has always been devoted to you. I am the adopted daughter of Janaka, the daughter of the Earth. Can you not believe my devotion and chastity?" she wailed.

Sita turned to Lakshmana and said, "Lakshmana, I cannot live as one who is considered tainted. My husband, who does not praise my virtues, has spoken unmentionable words to me in front of everyone. **Light the fire**." With her head bowed, Sita saluted Rama, the gods, and the guardians of the directions, and proclaimed, "If my heart has always worshipped Ramachandra, may Agni (Fire), the consumer of all, purify me!" Saying this, she walked into the flames. Everyone cried out in dismay. At that moment, **Brahma** stood before Rama and said, "Rama, you are the creator of the world. You are the supreme knower. Why do you stand by and watch? Why do you neglect Sita like an ordinary man?" He then revealed that Rama was an **avatar of Vishnu**.

Agni brought Sita back to Rama. Sita then shone like the rising sun. Agni said, "Rama! Here is your Sita. She is purified and free of sin. She is a virtuous woman who desired only you. You must accept her. Do not disobey me. I command you." Rama replied, "I know that Sita is supremely pure. But as the son of Dasaratha, I could not behave like one driven by lust. I silently witnessed the fire ordeal so that the world might recognize her greatness. Since you speak with affection for me, I will do as you say." He extended his right hand and accepted Sita's hand.

lessons.title: Lesson 19 — Return to Ayodhya
lessons.content:
At Rama's request, **Indra** revived all the dead Vanaras. The entire army was immersed in celebration. Rama, eager to reach Ayodhya, declined Vibhishana's honors. Vibhishana, with Rama's permission, honored the Vanaras. Accompanied by Vibhishana and the Vanaras, Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana began their return journey to Ayodhya on the **Pushpaka Vimana**. Along the way, they viewed the sites of their war in Lanka, Sita's abduction, and their life in the forest, crossing Kishkindha, the Godavari, the Yamuna, and the Ganga before reaching the hermitage of **Sage Bharadwaja**. At Rama's request, Sage Bharadwaja granted a boon that all the trees would bear sweet fruits, even out of season, for the joy of the Vanaras.

**Hanuman** was sent ahead to Nandigrama and delivered the message of Sita, Rama, and Lakshmana's return to **Bharata**. Bharata, filled with joy, ordered Ayodhya to be decorated. He placed Rama's sandals on his head and, accompanied by his retinue, went to meet them. He prostrated before Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana. He embraced Sugriva and the other heroes, declaring that due to their friendship, Sugriva was now their fifth brother. He stated that he had protected the kingdom in Rama's name and prayed that Rama would take back the burden of the state. He asked Rama to inspect the cowsheds, granaries, treasuries, and armies. With Bharata as the charioteer, Shatrughna holding the white umbrella, Lakshmana and Vibhishana fanning them with whisks, and the Vanara heroes following, Sita, Rama, and their entourage entered Ayodhya amidst the sound of conches and drums. They bowed to their mothers, elders, and gurus. The citizens of Ayodhya were astonished to hear the details of their time in the forest, the abduction of Sita, the friendship with Sugriva in Kishkindha, Hanuman's unparalleled achievement, Vibhishana's surrender, and the war in Lanka.
